Keywords: Can, Nothing, Chamber

outputs.L1:

A heart is merely a physical object, singing within the chest. Chamber doors oxygenating blood as it rushes through. Salmon climbing upstream through the river. It sounds like a grifter's hustle. Don't do it.

In any case, you attempt to place yourself within the experience of nature poetry. Yet even there, your mind keeps returning to how you dislike relieving yourself outdoors. You prefer a proper toilet, a stall, and toilet tissue. Your thoughts ruin beautiful poetic expressions with expressions of another kind before the flush. Indeed, upon viewing a nature painting, you find yourself scouting a suitable spot to relieve yourself—considering where to dig a hole and bury the evidence afterward, as a matter of courtesy. Some mass crushing the flowers beneath it. Or smeared across a granite slope. Is not a waterfall simply one continuous flush?

outputs.L2:
Soft sounds barely register when they're the whispering kind. No tenderness passed from palm to palm. Horsehair dragged across gut strings. The heart—just tissue and muscle, belting out a tune inside your ribcage. Blood pumping through valves like doors swinging open for air. Salmon fighting their way upstream. When someone describes light as though it were a grin painted onto a face, you call it garbage, that whole reading. A meme reshared endlessly, its image welded to some caption. Talk about the Soul? That's con-artist territory. Skip it. 

Regardless, you attempt to insert yourself into that nature-poem headspace. But once you're there, your brain keeps circling back to your aversion to outdoor bathroom breaks. You're a fan of porcelain thrones, stall doors, and proper toilet paper. Every gorgeous poetic phrase gets hijacked in your head by thoughts of what comes before flushing. Show you a landscape painting and you're scouting locations for relief. Digging a hole, covering it after—basic manners. Some poor patch of wildflowers getting flattened. Or streaked across some granite face. Isn't a waterfall basically nature's endless toilet flush? 

What you're getting at: if you could switch to black-light vision and see the truth—every surface coated in filth—this whole planet would radiate with an eerie kind of beauty.
outputs.L3:
# On the Body's Insistent Honesty

There is a particular kind of failure that occurs when we try to listen for the subtle, the whispered, the barely-there—because the body will not stop shouting. Subtle or whispered things are easily missed, drowned out by the relentless, physical fact of the heart: not a symbol, not a metaphor, but an actual singing muscle, a wet fist of tissue driving blood through the body's chambers with a rhythm that predates and outlasts every quiet thought we try to have. The heart doesn't whisper. It pumps. And in its pumping, it reminds us that we are, before anything else, meat that moves liquid through itself.

This insistence on the literal makes certain poetic gestures feel less like insight and more like sleight of hand. Poetic interpretations—comparing light to a painted smile, invoking something so slippery as "Soul"—start to look like dishonest or manipulative moves, the verbal equivalent of a grifter's hustle. The metaphor promises transcendence but delivers only a clever substitution, a shell game where the pea of actual experience has been swapped for something prettier and emptier. We are meant to feel elevated, but we've only been sold a costume.

Nowhere is this tension more evident than in the attempt to lose oneself in nature poetry. One tries to dissolve into the sublime—the rustling leaves, the ancient trees, the timeless mountain silence—but the mind, traitorous and grounded, keeps circling back to the body's practical concerns. A preference for toilets over outdoor defecation surfaces unbidden, absurd and insistent, refusing to be poeticized away. The forest floor is beautiful until you remember you'd rather not squat on it.

This bodily preoccupation doesn't just interrupt the poem—it infects it, transforming natural imagery from the inside out. A waterfall becomes, helplessly, a flush. The mind intrudes with thoughts of burying waste, of things washing away, of the body's outputs finding their place in the very systems the poet meant to sanctify. The sublime cannot fully exclude the scatological; they are, it turns out, drinking from the same river.

And yet there is a strange redemption lurking in this collision of the elevated and the crude. The text concludes with a surreal reframing: imagine the world under black-light vision, where every trace of waste, every hidden stain, becomes suddenly visible. In this vision, the world doesn't become uglier—it glows. If all waste were rendered luminous, the paradox suggests, we would finally see the world as it truly is: not despite its mess, but *because* of it—beautiful not in spite of the body's insistence, but through it.
outputs.L4:
# On the Poetry of Filth

There is a certain kind of language we reach for when we speak of nature—language soaked in reverence, dripping with metaphor. We speak of hearts that beat in time with tides, of souls illuminated by the same light that touches mountain peaks, of some grand correspondence between the inner life of the human spirit and the outer life of the world. The poets have trained us well. We learn to say "light" and mean something more than photons; we learn to say "soul" and mean something that exists nowhere in particular but everywhere we choose to feel it. This is the romantic inheritance: nature as mirror, nature as metaphor, nature as the screen upon which we project our most elevated selves.

But bodies do not care about metaphor.

The body that walks through the forest, moved to tears by dappled sunlight, is the same body that must, at some point, find a place to relieve itself. The soul that swells with cosmic connection while watching a sunset is housed in tissue that sweats, that sheds skin cells, that harbors bacteria, that will eventually need to wipe itself clean. This is not a cynical observation—it is simply true, and its truth sits uncomfortably alongside our poetic aspirations. We want nature to be sublime. We do not want to think about the fact that every deer in every dappled clearing is, at this moment, probably defecating somewhere nearby. We do not want to think about our own hygiene while we are busy having transcendent experiences.

This creates a peculiar kind of dishonesty in how we speak about the natural world. We edit out the physical facts that would puncture the mood. We speak of "hearts" and "light" and "souls" while carefully avoiding words like "waste," "decay," "excrement"—as though these were somehow separate from nature rather than fundamental to it. As though a forest could exist without decomposition, without the endless cycle of consumption and elimination that makes every ecosystem function.

But consider this thought experiment: imagine you had a strange kind of vision—call it black-light vision—that let you see all the waste in the world made suddenly visible, suddenly luminous. Every trace of urine on every tree trunk marking territory. Every pile of scat decomposing into soil. Every shed skin cell floating in every ray of sunlight. The world would suddenly reveal itself as absolutely covered in the residue of bodily existence—not as some horrifying revelation, but as a kind of glowing, alien landscape of biological truth.

And here is the strange turn: under this imagined light, the waste does not look ugly. It glows. It becomes its own kind of beauty—not despite being waste, but because it is waste, because it is evidence of the endless metabolic dance of living things processing the world and returning something to it. The urine-marked tree becomes a map of animal movement, a testament to territory and survival. The scattered scat becomes fertilizer, becomes the future soil that will feed future trees. The shed skin cells become part of the very dust that catches light and makes sunbeams visible in the first place.

This is not to say that we should abandon poetic language entirely, or that hearts and light and souls have no place in how we speak of nature. But perhaps authentic engagement with the natural world—and with our own animal bodies moving through it—requires holding both registers simultaneously. The transcendent and the mundane. The sublime and the scatological. We are creatures capable of profound aesthetic and spiritual experience precisely because we are creatures with bodies, and bodies are messy, leaking, excreting things.

To romanticize nature while pretending away its physical realities is to engage in a kind of sanitized fantasy—one that keeps us at a comfortable distance from what nature actually is. But to see the whole picture, waste included, illuminated under our imagined black light, is to discover that beauty was never about purity in the first place. It was always about the strange, glowing truth of things as they actually are: bodies among bodies, waste becoming soil becoming light becoming life again, in an endless cycle that includes us, fully, without exception, without the need for metaphor to make it bearable.
outputs.L5:
# The Empty Chamber

In the abandoned house at the end of the lane, there stood a chamber that time had forgotten. Dust motes drifted through shafts of afternoon light, settling on surfaces that hadn't been touched in years. The room was empty—or so it seemed at first glance.

On the windowsill sat a rusted tin can, its label long faded into illegibility. It seemed like such an insignificant object, yet it was the only thing that suggested someone had once lived here, had once eaten something from that can and left it behind, perhaps meaning to return for it.

Nothing else remained. No furniture, no photographs, no signs of the life that must have unfolded within these four walls. The chamber held its silence like a secret, offering nothing to explain who had been here or why they had left so abruptly.

I stood in the doorway, wondering what stories these walls could tell if they could speak. The can on the sill seemed to mock my curiosity—a small, stubborn relic refusing to give up its history. Perhaps that was the point. Perhaps some rooms are meant to hold their emptiness, their nothing, as a kind of quiet dignity.

I left the chamber as I found it, the can still resting in its place, a solitary witness to absence. Some questions, I realized, are better left unanswered. Some spaces deserve to keep their secrets, wrapped in the nothing that gives them their peculiar, haunting beauty.

**Digestive Ecology**

Morning comes like a bad decision, the sun hauling itself up over the horizon the way I haul myself off the toilet, both of us groaning under the weight of yesterday's choices, and I think about how the trees don't ask permission to drop their leaves in October, just let them fall wherever, littering lawns like my own hair in the shower drain, this slow autumn of the scalp, and somewhere a bird is singing about spring while I'm coughing up whatever's been living in my lungs since March, some phlegmy little ecosystem all its own, moss growing on the north side of my bronchi, and isn't that just like nature, doesn't ask if you're ready, the pollen doesn't check your allergies before it detonates yellow across the windshield, before it turns my sinuses into swampland, drip drip dripping like a leaky faucet nobody's fixed, like the gutter outside dumping rainwater onto the same patch of dirt until it's mud, until it's a small brown grave for grass, and I stand in my kitchen digesting last night's regret, whatever fermented in my stomach like compost, breaking down into something that might feed a garden if gardens ate shame, if roses bloomed on guilt instead of nitrogen, and the moon does whatever the moon does to the ocean, some tidal bullying, some gravitational bruise, and my body does whatever my body does to me, bloating and cramping in solidarity with the seasons, water retention like a drought-stricken reservoir deciding to hoard for once, and I sweat like the earth sweats humidity before a storm, salt crusting my shirt like frost on a windshield nobody scraped, and everything is just fluid dynamics really, blood and rain and bile and runoff, all of it moving downhill toward some ocean of used-up matter, all of it churning in the same stupid cycle, the worms eating the leaves eating the light eating whatever's left of me when this is over, dust to dust, shit to soil, the whole indifferent machinery grinding on, birds still singing, my stomach still counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental piece of writing that mocks traditional nature poetry while weaving in crude humor and physical sensation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to a Tick I Found in My Ass Crack After a "Peaceful" Hike

O Nature, thou vast and breathing cathedral,
thou green-fingered mother of all sighing leaves—
I came to thee seeking transcendence
and left thee with a parasite
burrowed into the sacred grove
of my nethermost regions.

Wordsworth never mentioned this part.

The brook did babble, yes, as brooks are known to do,
babbling in that self-satisfied way brooks have,
like they invented sound itself,
like they're not just water falling over rocks
being weird and wet and loud about it.
I sat beside it. I felt something profound.
Then a horsefly bit me on the eyelid
and the profundity evaporated
into a single-note scream
that echoed off the mountains
Nature had so generously provided
for scream-echoing purposes.

The mountains, majestic, purple-hued at dusk—
I want you to know I saw them.
I want you to know I also, at that exact moment,
felt my stomach do the thing
where the trail mix and the elevation gain
enter into a kind of theological argument
and I had to duck behind a juniper
that had clearly seen this before,
judging by the state of its lower branches.

The wind whispered secrets through the pines.
I whispered back, "please, God, not here,
not in front of the wind."

Let other poets speak of eagles.
Let them arc their words upward
toward talon and sky and the meaning of freedom.
I will speak instead of the squirrel
that watched me struggle out of my pack straps
with an expression of such total contempt
I understood, finally, my place
in the great chain of being:
somewhere below the squirrel.

And when the sun set—
oh, when the sun set, reader,
it set the way suns do, orange and huge
and dropping into the ridgeline
like it was tired of holding itself up all day,
which, honestly, mood—
I felt tears come to my eyes
that were probably alkaline dust
but let's call them tears, let's call it awe,
let's call the ache in my hips
and the sunburn on the back of my neck
and the tick, God, the tick,
already three days into its lease agreement
before I even found it—

let's call all of it beautiful.
Because it was.
It was beautiful and it hurt like hell
and I would, appallingly, go back tomorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something surreal and darkly funny about experiencing nature but being unable to stop thinking about needing to poop.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Vista

The canyon opened before him like something out of a religious painting—layers of red and gold stratified by ten thousand years of patient erosion, the kind of view that made people whisper about God or at least Ansel Adams.

Gerald whispered, "Not now. Not now not now not now."

His bowels disagreed. They had opinions. They had been forming these opinions since mile marker three, and now, at the scenic overlook, at the apex of the trail, at the precise moment his wife turned to him with tears in her eyes and said "isn't it magnificent," his intestines began to compose an epic poem in a language only he could understand, and its subject was *urgency*.

"It's magnificent," he agreed, buttocks clenched with the concentration of a man defusing a bomb.

A hawk drifted on a thermal below them—*below* them, that's how high up they were, close enough to touch the ceiling of heaven—and Gerald thought: there is no bathroom for four miles. There is no bathroom for four miles and I contain multitudes and all of them need to leave immediately.

"Do you feel small?" his wife asked. "Insignificant? Like a tiny speck against the vastness of time?"

"Yes," Gerald said, and he did, he really did, he felt like a tiny speck being crushed by a vastness of an entirely different nature, a vastness located approximately eight inches from his exit.

The canyon had been carved by the Colorado River over six million years. Gerald had approximately six minutes.

He thought about the pioneers. The pioneers had crossed this exact land in wagons, with dysentery, with nothing but a shovel and their dignity, and they had *survived*, and surely he could survive one photo opportunity, surely—

"Smile!" said his wife.

He smiled. Somewhere in the earth's crust, tectonic plates shifted with more subtlety than what was happening in Gerald's abdomen.

The camera clicked. The hawk cried out—a sound like the void calling back to something even more empty—and Gerald understood, in that suspended, terrible moment, that nature did not care about his colon. Nature had never cared. Nature would erode this canyon for another six million years, indifferent, eternal, while he stood here haunted by a Clif Bar he shouldn't have eaten and a bathroom that did not exist.

"I love you," his wife said.

"I love you too," Gerald said, already walking, already calculating trail speed versus structural integrity, already becoming one with the landscape in a way no ranger pamphlet had ever warned him about.

The canyon watched him go, ancient, patient, magnificent.

It had seen this before.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of abstract, anti-lyrical prose that critiques the pretentiousness of "soul" language in poetry, blending visceral bodily imagery with meditations on sound and light.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Alleged Interior**

The soul, they keep saying, as if pointing to a room no one has entered, as if the word were a key rather than a stain spreading on the ceiling where the pipes have gone. I am tired of the word soul doing all that unpaid labor, propping up every third stanza like a crutch under a leg that was never broken, just lazy, just fond of the shape of limping.

Here is what I have instead: cartilage. The gristle at the knee that pops when weather turns. A tongue that tastes its own iron before it tastes anything else. You want transcendence—I'll give you the wet click of a jaw unhinging to yawn, the small tragedy of a hangnail. This is not less profound. This is what is actually here, actually humming.

Light does not illuminate the soul. Light hits a retina, a wet disc no bigger than a coin, and the disc sends its frantic electric gossip down a wire made of meat to a lump of grey fat that decides, arbitrarily, to call this "seeing." There is no light of understanding. There is only cone and rod, chemical and charge. The rest is décor. The rest is what poets hang on the walls of the skull to make the apartment look lived-in.

Sound: not the "music of being," not some celestial string vibrating in the diaphragm of the universe—just air, compressed and rude, slapping the eardrum like a screen door in wind. When I hear a voice I love I do not hear a soul singing to my soul. I hear pressure waves shoving against a drum of skin stretched tight as a fist, and somewhere behind that drum, three tiny bones named for a hammer, an anvil, a stirrup, doing manual labor no one thanks them for. It is industrial. It is plumbing. Call it beautiful if you like—it is beautiful precisely because it is plumbing, because nothing had to reach beyond the skull's own wet machinery to make me weep.

I am suspicious of any poem that arrives already dressed for church. I want the poem that arrives late, sweating, with a stain on its collar, saying: I don't know what happens after the body stops, I only know this body, now, its spit and gray hairs and the ache behind the sternum that might be grief or might be gas. Stop calling that soul. Call it the ache behind the sternum. Let the mystery live in the not-knowing, not in the borrowed vocabulary of stained glass.

Some nights the moon comes up looking like a knuckle, swollen, and I could say *soul* and mean nothing, or I could say *knuckle* and mean the moon, mean the hand, mean the small violence of being struck by beauty the way a body is struck—directly, physically, leaving a mark that will yellow, then fade, then vanish, the way everything real does, without ascending anywhere at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a weird, unfiltered internal monologue of someone standing in a beautiful landscape, distracted by bathroom anxieties, ending with a bizarre black-light metaphor about waste covering the world.
counterfactuals.output:
Okay. Okay, this is—god, look at that. The way the light hits the ridge there, gold going to purple, like someone bruised the sky on purpose and it healed beautiful. This is the kind of thing you're supposed to feel something about. Smallness. Awe. The vastness of it all humbling your little animal heart.

But did I actually lock the car.

The valley opens up below like a green throat and I'm thinking about my throat, and my stomach, which has been making a sound like a distant argument for the last twenty minutes. Not urgent. Not yet. But present. A rumor of urgency. The mountains have stood here for ten thousand years completely unbothered and I have been alive for thirty-four and already my body is drafting a complaint.

There's a hawk up there. Circling. Probably doesn't think about bathrooms. Probably has never once in its life thought "is there a bathroom" while looking at something transcendent. Just eats a vole and lets it fly out the back end mid-flight, no shame, no scouting for cover, no mental inventory of the last place with a door that locks. Must be nice. Truly the freedom of the skies.

The wind smells like pine and cold rock and something mineral, ancient, like the inside of the earth exhaling, and I am standing in it thinking: how far is the trailhead. Not "how far" in a spiritual sense. In a "is there a vault toilet within a reasonable jog" sense. I did the math already, twice. It's not good math.

This is supposed to be a moment. I drove two hours for this moment. The light is doing the thing where it turns the granite the color of a peach, of a wound, of communion wine, and some part of me — some good, uncorrupted, poetic part — is trying to just have the experience, just be here, and the other part, the louder part, the part that has apparently been running this whole show since childhood, is doing inventory. Water bottle: half full, don't drink more. Stomach: rumor becoming rumor with citations. Distance to anything resembling privacy: not close enough.

And then, because my brain does this, because my brain is a haunted house with too many rooms, it goes somewhere stupid. It goes: what if you could see it. All of it. Every trace everybody's ever left, glowing. Like a crime scene. Like they spray that blue light and the invisible comes up neon.

What if the whole world was like that. Every trail, every gas station bathroom, every bush behind every scenic overlook, every ocean, every single square foot humans have ever passed through — lit up under some cosmic black light, all our leavings fluorescing at once. The Sistine Chapel glowing faintly where some Renaissance guy had to go and held it through four saints and an archangel. Everest base camp lit up like a rave. The ocean floor a soft toxic green from centuries of ships just doing what ships do. The whole earth wearing us like a stain, glowing, humming, an atlas of everybody's worst-timed emergencies, all of it fluorescent and undeniable and strangely, horribly beautiful, like the world's largest and least consensual art installation, WASTE: A RETROSPECTIVE, curated by every living thing that ever ate something and then, later, had feelings about it.

The hawk's still up there. The light's still doing the thing.

I really do need to find a bathroom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
